**Relevant information:**
- In our conversation on 22 May 2023, I summarized the "Experimental Results" section of the "To Adapt or Not to Adapt? Real-Time Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation" submission.
- That summary said the HAMLET framework improved the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency in online domain adaptation.
- It also gave the framerate gains:
  - The Hardware-Aware Modular Training (HAMT) agent gave an average framerate improvement of **about 20%**.
  - Adding the Active Training Modulation system gave a further improvement of about 4x.
- These results came from the OnDA benchmarks and the SHIFT dataset.

**Answer:** Using the HAMT agent improved the framerate by about **20%** on average. Adding the Active Training Modulation system then brought a further gain of about 4x.

2. **Answer:** The average improvement in framerate when using the **HAMT agent alone was approximately 20%**.

**Relevant information:** Item 1 is the only one that concerns the "To Adapt or Not to Adapt? Real-Time Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation" submission. Its "Experimental Results" section says the HAMLET framework significantly improved the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency in online domain adaptation. It reports "an average improvement in framerate of approximately 20% when using the Hardware-Aware Modular Training (HAMT) agent." It adds that the Active Training Modulation system gave a further improvement of approximately 4x.

**Reasoning:** The question asks about the average framerate improvement from the HAMT agent alone. The 4x figure comes from adding Active Training Modulation, so it does not apply here. The HAMT figure is about 20%.

**Answer:** The HAMT agent gave an average framerate improvement of approximately 20%.
